subject: chemistry
title: Tiny Particles Everywhere
welcome_lead: Zoom in past the eye's limit and find the secret world of particles.
meta_desc: Discover the particle model in this KS3 chemistry adventure on tiny building blocks of matter.
final_note: You can now picture matter as countless tiny moving particles.

walkthroughs.body_html:
The particle model says that everything is made of tiny particles too small to see — even with a microscope.

All matter = lots of particles.

The model explains the three states beautifully:

Solid — particles tightly packed in a regular pattern, only vibrating.
Liquid — close together, sliding past each other.
Gas — far apart, moving quickly and randomly.
Heating a substance gives particles more energy, so they move faster. Eventually they have enough energy to break free from their neighbours — and the substance changes state.

All matter is made of tiny particles
Only solids have particles

options: They stop moving
They move faster
They become smaller
Nothing changes

mcqs.q: What is the role of the fingerprint region (below ~1500 cm^-1) in IR spectroscopy?
options: The fingerprint region is the part that contains all the most useful absorptions.
It is unique to each compound — used to identify a specific molecule by matching to a known spectrum.
The fingerprint region is used to identify which functional groups are present.
The M+ peak shows the mass of a single hydrogen atom added to the molecule.

mcqs.q: What does the M+ peak in a mass spectrum represent?
options: The M+ peak shows the mass of a single hydrogen atom added to the molecule.
The molecular ion — formed when a single electron is removed from the whole molecule, giving the relative molecular mass.
The M+ peak shows the mass of the largest fragment after the molecule breaks apart.
The fingerprint region is the part that contains all the most useful absorptions.

mcqs.q: When water boils, what is broken?
options: The covalent bonds between hydrogen and oxygen atoms are broken when water boils.
The M+ peak shows the mass of a single hydrogen atom added to the molecule.
Intermolecular forces (hydrogen bonds) between water molecules are broken — the O-H covalent bonds stay intact.
Water molecules split into hydrogen and oxygen gas when they boil.
